newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to clear aid to German, Spanish, Greek yards.
newsitem.headline: EU to clear aid to German, Spanish, Greek yards.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to clear on Wednesday new German subsidies amounting to 728 million marks ($436 million) to help two shipyards in former east Germany which were previously owned by bankrupt Bremer Vulkan, EU sources said on Tuesday.
The Commission will also allow the Greek government to write off 54.5 billion drachmas ($206 million) in debts accumulated by the Hellenic shipyards before it was privatised in September 1995.
Finally, the Commission will approve 135 billion pesetas ($948 million) in aid for restructuring publicly owned yards in Spain.

The yards in the three countries have in common that previous measures to bring them back to profit failed. The Commission's competition services found that they all presented a good case for additional subsidies, but warned this should be the last time, the sources said.
"There were exceptional circumstances which explain that the existing plans did not work," an EU official said.

This was particularly the case for the German yards MTW-Schiffswerft and Volkswerft Stralsund whose woes arise directly from the misuse by their parent company Bremer Vulkan of subsidies intended for them. The Commission found last year that MTW and Volkswerft had been deprived respectively of 580 million marks and 270 million marks by Vulkan.

The sources said that to compensate for this, the German authorities had agreed new aid measures totalling 1.04 billion marks for the two yards located in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on the Baltic sea coast.
The Commission only had a say on operating and social aid which amounts to 333 million for MTW and 395 million for Volkswerft, they said.
The plans for the yards in the three countries will be submitted to EU industry ministers at their next scheduled meeting on April 24.
In the case of the Hellenic yards, the aid was justified by successive delays in privatising the company, something which was supposed to happen early in 1993.
The yards were partly sold to its workers more than two years later. The Greek government kept a majority stake of 51 percent for defence interests.

Aid to Spanish yards in Seville and Santander was to cover interest payments of up to 62 billion pesetas between 1988 and 1994 on loans taken out to cover previously approved subsidies which were never paid, the sources said.
A further 58 billion pesetas was tax credits in the period 1995-1999 and a capital injection of up to 15 billion pesetas this year.

The sources said that in return for the new measures, the Commission had obtained capacity cuts in Spain and Germany. $1 = 1.67 marks $1 = 264.4 drachmas $1 = 142 pesetas -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
